To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the electrochemical oxidation kinetics and susceptibility of the basal surface of HOPG to fouling are independent of the method of cleavage (e.g., cleavage in air or under vacuum) and step edge density (e.g., high or low step edge density), and that the pristine basal surface of HOGP is the most active carbon surface termination for the electrochemical detection of DA in the submicromolar range, irrespective of the method of preparation and step edge density, with a fast response

the electrochemical oxidation kinetics of DA are fast on basal plane HOPGs, with little indication that surface fouling by DA oxidation products occurs, and the electrochemical response for DA can be resolved from the background signal at concentrations <10 μM.

the basal plane surface of HOPG (independent of cleavage method) is an excellent surface for the detection of low concentrations of dopamine in the presence of ascorbic acid, and that the electrochemical oxidation kinetics of dopamine is very fast and the electrode surface is not easily passivated by the oxidation products of DA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the electrochemical detection of neurotransmitters, in particular dopamine.

the electrochemical oxidation and voltammetric detection (in the presence of AA and 5-HT) of DA at the surface of a range of carbon electrodes, with particular emphasis on the pristine basal plane of HOGP, which has been largely overlooked in the past.

the development of a highly sensitive and selective voltammetric method for the detection of dopamine (DA), which is one of the major neurotransmitters in mammalian brain, and is also an important biomarker for Parkinson's disease and related disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, of all the carbon electrode surfaces studied, the basal plane surface of HOPG shows the greatest promise for the detection of trace amounts of dopamine in the presence of AA and 5-HT, although pBDD is also highly active and shows a much lower background signal.
the pristine surface basal plane HOPGs is the best electrode for the voltammetry of dopamine.
the electrochemical oxidation kinetics of DA at basal plane graphite is faster than at any other carbon electrode investigated in this work.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the basal plane surface of graphite, when carefully prepared, is an excellent choice for the electrochemical detection of DA, with a low susceptibility toward fouling from oxidation products, and a high sensitivity at low concentrations of this important neurotransmitter.
, in the presence of a permselective layer of AA oxidation products, basal plane HOPGs are the most promising electrodes for the voltammetric detection of dopamine.

the electrochemical oxidation and voltammetric detection (and quantification) of dopamine can be achieved with high sensitivity and selectivity on the pristine basal plane of highly oriented pyrolitic graphite (HOP) at concentrations as low as 1 μM, even in the presence of ascorbic acid and serotonin, which is relevant to neurochemical analysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

HOPG can be used to detect DA with high selectivity and sensitivity, and that the surface of HOPG can also be used as a template for the fabrication of more complex electrode structures, such as nanocomposites with conducting polymers, which may be useful in the fabrication of biosensors.
HOPG surfaces are much more active than GC for the detection of low concentrations of DA, and that this activity is largely independent of the surface step edge density.

, while pBDD is the most stable electrode for the detection of dopamine (and other electroactive species) in terms of surface passivation, it is also one of the least active electrodes, and therefore, the electrochemical oxidation kinetics of DA is much faster on HOPG.
